title: Fleet Co-Pilot
description: Cockpit incident tagging, live telemetry, and ODD coverage for an autonomous test fleet — plus the office dashboard engineers review it in.
hmw: trust an autonomous test fleet enough to scale it, without losing the edge cases only a safety driver ever sees?

facts.label: Platforms
facts.value: Flutter cockpit HUD (iOS/Android) + React fleet dashboard (web)

facts.label: Role
facts.value: End-to-end: cockpit UI, data taxonomy, office dashboard

blocks.text: Every surface — cockpit, hazard map, office dashboard — reads from the same six primitives, styled consistently wherever they appear.

image.alt: Fleet Co-Pilot design system: components and colors

blocks.text: One taxonomy from cockpit to office means no translation loss between what a driver saw and what an engineer reviews — the pattern autofleet’s safety-driver app and disengagement metrics point at.
Severity and subsystem are tagged at the moment of the event, not reconstructed later — the edge-case and video-snippet tagging digitaldividedata builds for AV footage retrieval.

Day/night/rain/traffic pass tracking against campaign targets makes exposure auditable, not anecdotal — operational exposure analysis and compliance/audit automation, both flagged across the research.
Owned end-to-end design for Fleet Co-Pilot, spanning the cockpit HUD, the incident taxonomy, and the office review dashboard that shares it.

Subsystem × severity (perception, motion planner, localization, hardware/sensor, ODD boundary × SEV1–3) powers the driver’s 1-tap tags, the hazard map, and the office incident log — no re-mapping between tools.
Grounded every decision in how autonomy and fleet-ops teams actually work:

items: Safety drivers need sub-second quick-tags, not forms
Ops and AV engineers need exposure and disengagement analytics after the fact
Compliance needs an audit trail, not tribal knowledge

blocks.text: Proved the taxonomy before building a backend for it:

items: Cockpit fixture data first, labeled simulated until a real ingestion pipeline exists
The office dashboard built as a second, independent consumer of the same schema
Validated the taxonomy held up outside the vehicle, not just inside it

blocks.text: Surveyed how autonomous-fleet operators actually run this today:

items: Multi-vendor AV monitoring and safety-driver incident apps
Operational exposure analysis and edge-case/video tagging

blocks.text:
Phantom Brake, Planner Freeze, Sensor Drop: three quick-tag buttons that log a subsystem and severity the instant something feels off, without pulling a driver’s eyes off the road.
The same pattern autofleet’s research flags as essential for safety-driver apps: incident reporting has to be faster than the incident.
Everything a safety driver sees, structured

Autonomy state, jerk, lateral g, time-to-collision, and headway gap sit next to the driver-monitoring read: gaze, drowsiness score, hands-on-wheel, and takeover reaction latency.
Nothing here is inferred after the fact — it’s the same read the safety driver had, timestamped.
Every disengagement becomes a place on the map

Fault and disengagement hotspots are geotagged with road segment, heading, and prior-disengagement count, then surfaced as an upcoming-hazard countdown as the vehicle approaches them again.
A tunnel that lost GPS once is a place the whole fleet gets warned about next time.

Day, night, rain/wet, and dense-traffic passes track against a per-route campaign target, so ODD coverage is a number, not a feeling.
Write rate, storage used, and sensor-stream sync status ride alongside it, so nothing gets logged in the cockpit and lost before it reaches the office.
